messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

Im new to this and not very proficient in R, but learning!

I'm running a single species multi season model. I have 2 primary occasions (summer and winter) and 4 secondary occasions (a week was considered a sampling unit).
I set up cameras and bait at each site, however only baited at the beginning of each season due to logistic reasons..
How may I test if detection and occupancy decrease or do not change across surveys due to bait deterioration?

Any suggestions would really help!

Cheers

messages.subject: Re: Incorporating bait deterioration in model?
messages.subject_clean: Incorporating bait deterioration in model?
messages.body_plain:
Interesting question, Riana.

Unless the bait is strong enough to attract movement in and out of each site (however defined), then its presence or deterioration shouldn't have any effect on occupancy (either initial occupancy or in colonization/extinction between summer and winter).

However, it makes sense that state of bait deterioration would influence your likelihood of attraction (and detection via cameras). You would, I'd think, need to quantify (or at least estimate) this state of deterioration to best use it as an observation/detection covariate (obsCov in an occu() or colext() model). For example, if it deteriorates in mass by half the amount per sampling week (assuming mass is relevant), you'd use a vector like c(1,0.5,0.25,0.125). There are lots of examples in this group and online for creating obsCovs.

You didn't go into your overall study design, but (assuming this is a mammal you're modeling) you should also make sure a multi-season (vs. single season) model is most appropriate.

Best, Giancarlo

Hello Ellery,

Let me see if I can help a little bit. Are the other s1 and s3, visual surveys? I think as you said there could be problems trying to relate detection covariates across different methods when not accounting for the differences in the methods. There is a paper, Nichols et al. 2008 that fits multi-method/multi-scale occupancy models that could be useful. Did you also conduct a visual survey during s2 when you took your eDNA sample? Depending on what questions you are interested in with this project, you could use your visual surveys with 3 replicate surveys in a single season occupancy model with the detection covariates of interest. Then in a separate single season model use your eDNA survey which is really 3 temporal replicates of the site (sample 1, 2, and 3) same as the visual surveys. This way you could incorporate detection covariates that are more appropriate for the particular method. Both models should address occupancy across the sites but using different methods where you could compare detection probabilities. I think this is what Brittany was getting at as well.

Best,
Matt

messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,
I'm posting this as a follow-up to a previous post (which I have deleted as I was able to answer my question on my own before anyone was able to respond) and have since come up with more specific and detailed questions to resulting issues.

Some quick background info:

We had 3 observers conduct 3 rounds of 10-min long point-count surveys at 150 points (i.e. each observer visited each point once) over 10 weeks. The species we are working with has a high tendency to flock together, so rather than record distances for individual birds we recorded distances to the center of each cluster per recommendations from Buckland et al (cluster size ranged from 1-14 individuals with a mean of~3).

My first question is in regards to how I should handle the fact that I'm working with clusters and which function I should use to do so as I expect that cluster size is likely to be one of the most important covariates affecting detection. My first thought was model detection of clusters and then use cluster size as a covariate, rather than model detection of individuals. For example my observation data from point 1 would look something like:

Point            Observation           Distance            Cluster_Size
1                  1                            46                       1
1                  1                            87                       4

Rather than:

Point            Observation           Distance
1                  1                             46
1                  4                             87

I would then try to estimate the total abundance of clusters across my study region and extrapolate that out to abundance of individuals using either mean cluster size or a size-biased regression analysis similar to what is possible with Program Distance. However, my understanding is that doing it this way would require coding cluster size as an observation level covariate. From what I've been able to glean from the help files and vignettes I can only include observation level covariates if I use colext(), gmultmix(), or gpcount() and the associated unmarkedFrames. However, because I had repeated visits to each site and have distance data I feel like I should be using gdistsamp() for all of my analyses, which I don't think can incorporate observation level covariates (though please correct me if I'm wrong!!!!).

Question 1:

Is taking this approach and modeling detection of clusters rather than individuals appropriate, and if so what function should I use/how should I structure my data to do so given that I would like to model cluster size as a covariate and used a repeated visits design? Can any function in unmarked handle both repeated visits and observation level covariates for distance data?

My second question has to do with some funky results I keep getting in my preliminary analyses, I should note that this pattern keeps occurring regardless of whether I try to model detection of clusters (which I have done but have not been able to incorporate cluster size as a covariate into the model yet) or model detection of individuals. In general models using a negative binomial mixture consistently out-perform those using poisson. In many ways I expected this outcome, especially since my data has a LOT of 0 observations, which is partly why repeated visits were necessary. Top ranking models using the NB also do well on bootstrapped GoF tests (specifically Freeman-Tukey). However, the density/abundance estimates I get from using NB mixtures are all unreasonably high (i.e. ~10X the upper limit of what I would expect). In previous discussions I have seen some people mention that this can occur when using NB, and even found a comment from one contributor referencing a paper by Johnson circa 2009 from Conservation Biology that discusses this issue, but have been unable to find said paper and am unclear on why this happens with NB or what to do about it.

Question 2:
Why are my abundance estimates with negative binomial ~10X larger than the ones I'm getting from poisson, and does anyone have any advice for what I should do to address this problem? My impression from working with these birds is that despite the large number of 0 observations detectability is fairly high but availability extremely low, would accounting for availability resolve this problem or should I ignore NegBin entirely despite the fact that for some reasons it seems appropriate?

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated, and thanks for any help.

Best,
Nathaniel

messages.body_plain:
We am trying to build a species based site occupancy model but our observers might be slightly different from the normal set of observers because they are either “perfect” observers (e.g. they identify the species in all sites) or they are “terrible” observers (e.g. they never identify the species in all sites). I haven’t been able to find any indications this should be a problem in either MacKenzie et al. 2006 “Occupancy Estimation and Modeling” or Kery and Royle 2016: “Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology”, BUT we get the Error message: “Hessian is singular. Try providing starting values or using fewer covariates.”.

Hi Nathaniel, (quick responses in bold)

 However, because I had repeated visits to each site and have distance data I feel like I should be using gdistsamp() for all of my analyses, which I don't think can incorporate observation level covariates (though please correct me if I'm wrong!!!!).

I believe that in gdistsamp, yearlySiteCovs (one input for the frame) can act as obsCovs...ie., yearly site covs can vary by visit.

Question 2:
Why are my abundance estimates with negative binomial ~10X larger than the ones I'm getting from poisson, and does anyone have any advice for what I should do to address this problem? My impression from working with these birds is that despite the large number of 0 observations detectability is fairly high but availability extremely low, would accounting for availability resolve this problem or should I ignore NegBin entirely despite the fact that for some reasons it seems appropriate?

If you have AHM vol 1., there's a good section describing trade-offs between Neg-Bin and Poisson (I think in the N-mixture chapter). Negative Binomial mixtures often fit the data better, but can also result in strange estimates.  A strongly Zero-inflated Poission distribution has extra Poisson variability -> Poor Poisson fit -> NegBinomial selection, even though NegBin may not be a realistic assumed distribution--the paper I think you are looking for is by Joseph et al. 2009 (Ecological Applications).  NBin might well describe the flock-size fairly well, but your description suggests that it may not describe the 'abundance' of flocks all that well.

I don't know that incorporating availability will 'fix' issues of abundance estimation, but it does provide a little more flexibility for thinking about how abundance might be interpreted.

Is taking this approach and modeling detection of clusters rather than individuals appropriate...?

Punting on this. A more complex approach that comes to mind might involve working with spatial distance model (maybe the underlying point process describing individual locations is over-dispersed), but this seems like a tricky problem (Abundance influences detection influences estimation of abundance). Treating flock size as influencing detection makes sense (don't know whether a covariate, or an off-set, or some other functional relationship is best). I'd just suggest that for trying to get at overall bird population size by multiplying the estimated number of flocks by average cluster size or whatever, that the observed flocks seem likely to be bigger than the flocks missed.

John

Dear Marc

Thank you very much for the reply – and sorry if I didn’t describe the problem clearly. So its not that they identify species in all sites within the total area of interest (S) – only all the sites they visit (s) which is a smaller fraction of the total number of sites in the study area. For the individual sites there will be some with no detection at all, and some where all observers surveying found the species – and everything in between.

Thus, for sites (rows), there will be 1s = species observed, 0s = species not observed and NAs = observer didn’t survey the site.

But, for the individual observer (columns) there will be two distinct types: observer 1: only 1s or NAs and observer 2: only 0s or NAs.

I haven’t been able to find any indication this should cause problems, but imputing variability in the columns/observers does led to the model running.

Best, Jonas

Hi Heidi,

this is indeed a limitation in the current release of camtrapR, but here's a simple workaround.

You wrote:

I believe it's because my camop_no_problem was created with the variable byCamera as I had more than one camera at each station. So the camop_no_problem first column looks like this:
TrapName_CameraName

while my recordtable Station column only has
TrapName

This is exactly what is happening here. So you could create a new column in recordTable which combines station and camera IDs and corresponds to the values stationCol of recordTable. Can be achived by:

recordtable$StationCam <- paste(recordtable$Station, recordTable$Camera, sep = "_")

Afterwards, the IDs should match and detectionHistory should be happy. Please note that from camtrapR 0.99.6 (on CRAN since 20 Dec 2016) station and camera IDs are separated by 2 underscores ("__") to prevent problems in case you have underscores in your station or camera IDs.

But even if you have more than 1 camera at a station, you may wish to consider treating them as one station by setting byCamera = FALSE in function "cameraOperation" (e.g. if 2 cameras faced each other).

Hi all,
I am normally a Presence user but decided to use Unmarked for an analysis because I want to run the same set of models with many different occupancy data sets which would take forever in Presence.
